lines.speaker: Crates
lines.text: Did you know Moerichus, Diogenes? The rich Moerichus? Very rich, from Corinth, the one with the merchant fleet? Had a cousin named Aristeas who was just as wealthy? The one who was always quoting that line from Homer—'Either you lift me, or I lift you'?

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Why was he quoting that, Crates?

lines.speaker: Crates
lines.text: They were exactly the same age, and they were courting each other for the inheritance. It was a wrestling match of wills—literally. They put them on public display: Moerichus named Aristeas his sole heir if he died first, and Aristeas did the exact same for Moerichus. Then the flattery really started. They were trying to out-sycophant each other. Even the professionals got involved—astrologers, dream-readers, the Chaldeans, even the oracle at Delphi. One day the odds favored Aristeas, the next day Moerichus. The balance just kept tipping back and forth.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: So who won? [pause] It actually sounds worth hearing.

lines.speaker: Crates
lines.text: They died on the same day. The estates went to Eunomius and Thrasycles—a couple of distant relatives who never saw it coming. The two heirs-apparent were sailing from Sicyon to Cirrha, caught a crosswind off the Iapyx, and capsized.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: [laughs] Good for them. You know, when we were alive, we never thought about each other like that. I never prayed for Antisthenes to drop dead so I could inherit his walking stick—even though it was a very nice, sturdy piece of wild olive. And I don't suppose you, Crates, were desperately hoping for me to die so you could inherit my barrel and my knapsack with the two handfuls of lupine beans.

lines.speaker: Crates
lines.text: I didn't need them. Neither did you, Diogenes. You inherited everything that mattered from Antisthenes, and I inherited it from you. Wealth much greater and far more impressive than the whole Persian Empire.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Ah, yes. By Zeus, I do remember inheriting that particular fortune from Antisthenes, and leaving you even more than I started with.

lines.speaker: Crates
lines.text: But nobody else cared about that kind of property. Nobody ever sucked up to us hoping to be in our wills. They only had eyes for the gold.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Well, naturally. Even if we'd tried to leave them anything, they had nowhere to put it. They were entirely rotted out by luxury, like a threadbare coin-purse. You drop a little wisdom or frankness or truth into them, and it falls straight through. The bottom's completely gone. Like the daughters of Danaus trying to fill a sieve. But gold? They'll guard that with their teeth and nails and every dirty trick they know.

lines.speaker: Crates
lines.text: So here we are, still enjoying our wealth. While they arrive carrying exactly one obol—and they only get to keep that until they see the ferryman.
